title: Director, OWCP v. Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co. (1995)
shortTitle: Director, OWCP v. Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co.
summary: An agency administering a benefits statute is not a person adversely affected or aggrieved by an adjudicative ruling and cannot appeal it unless Congress specifically grants that right.
notes:
Key line: "Agencies do not automatically have standing to sue for actions that frustrate the purposes of their statutes." Justice Scalia, for the Court.

Citation: 514 U.S. 122 (1995).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was the Director of the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs in the Department of Labor, who administers the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act and who sought to appeal a ruling denying full benefits to a worker. Respondents were Newport News Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co., the employer, and its insurer. Jackie Harcum, the injured employee, did not appeal and expressly declined to intervene when the Fourth Circuit asked. The Director argued that her interest in ensuring correct payments to claimants and in administering the Act made her aggrieved by the ruling.
sections.Material Facts: On October 24, 1984, Harcum was working in the bilge of a steam barge at the Newport News shipyard when a piece of metal grating fell and struck his lower back, requiring surgery for a herniated disc. The company paid benefits until he returned to light-duty work in April 1987 and then to his regular department under medical restrictions in November 1987; it fired him in May 1988 when he could not perform essential tasks, and he found new work in February 1989. An administrative law judge held after a hearing on October 20, 1989 that Harcum was partially rather than totally disabled during his unemployment. The Benefits Review Board affirmed and added that the company could stop payments after 104 weeks, after which the special fund would pay. Section 21(c) of the Act, 33 U.S.C. 921(c), allows any person adversely affected or aggrieved by a Board order to seek review in the court of appeals.
sections.Procedural History: The Director petitioned the Fourth Circuit for review of the Board's decision. Harcum did not appeal and declined to intervene. Acting on its own motion, the Fourth Circuit held that the Director lacked standing because she was not adversely affected or aggrieved within section 21(c), and it dismissed the petition. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on January 9, 1995, and affirmed on March 21, 1995.
sections.Issue: Section 21(c) of the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act permits any person adversely affected or aggrieved by a final order of the Benefits Review Board to seek review in the court of appeals. The Director, who administers the Act, sought review of a ruling denying a worker full benefits even though the worker did not appeal and declined to intervene. Is the Director of the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs a person adversely affected or aggrieved under section 21(c), so that she may seek judicial review of a Board decision on the ground that it misapplies the statute she administers?
sections.Holding: No. The phrase adversely affected or aggrieved is a term of art describing private parties with a concrete stake, and no case has held that an agency acting as regulator or administrator falls within it without specific authorization. The Director's general interest in adequate payments and in administering the Act does not make her aggrieved by a ruling against a claimant who chose not to appeal. The judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Scalia began with the history of the phrase. Since the 1930s, adversely affected or aggrieved has designated persons with standing to appeal agency action, and it has never been read to include an agency in its governmental capacity absent express authorization. The APA itself uses the phrase and excludes agencies from the definition of person, and when Congress wants an agency to have standing it says so, as it did for the Secretary of Labor under OSHA. Nothing in the Longshore Act's text gave the phrase a special meaning. The Court then rejected the Director's two asserted interests. Agencies do not automatically have standing to sue whenever a ruling frustrates the purposes of their statutes; unless Congress confers a clear responsibility to vindicate a class of interests, private interests are left to private parties, and Harcum had chosen not to appeal. The Director's claimed interest in administering the Act was too abstract; she identified no specific statutory duty that the Board's ruling interfered with, only conjectural harms. The Court declined to expand agency authority in the name of statutory purposes, because every statute pursues its ends through particular means and the withholding of agency power is as deliberate as its grant.

topics.lrs-n-standing-apa702: Language about aggrieved persons does not necessarily authorize an agency policymaker’s appeal.
topics.lrs-n-standing-zone: The Court read 'person adversely affected or aggrieved' as a term of art requiring an interest of the kind the statute protects, not a general policy interest in the program's administration, which parallels the zone-of-interests analysis under APA § 702.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was unanimous. Justice Ginsburg concurred in the judgment, observing that the result created a disparity between the Longshore Act and the Black Lung Benefits Act, under which the Director has been permitted to appeal, and suggesting that Congress could correct it.
